content.title: Arkansas basketball blown out in season-ending loss to Arizona
content.text: SAN JOSE, Calif. — For the second year in a row, the Arkansas men’s basketball team saw its season end at the Sweet 16. But unlike last year's overtime loss to Texas Tech in nearby San Francisco, it wasn’t close this time around at the West Regional. Top-seeded Arizona imposed its will offensively and downed the fourth-seeded Razorbacks 109-88 to advance to the Elite Eight for the first time since 2015.The Wildcats (35-2) will face Purdue with a Final Four trip on the line Saturday at 7:49 p.m. Central on TBS. The second-seeded Boilermakers defeated 11th-seeded Texas 79-77 on a last-second make by Trey Kaufman-Wren in the early game Thursday at SAP Center.The Razorbacks (28-9) had a seven-game win streak snapped to end what tied for the winningest season since the 1994-95 team finished as national runner-up with a 32-7 record. “I told my team after, I'm proud of them [and] what they did this year,” Arkansas coach John Calipari said. “And I don't want them to look at one game and take away from what they've all accomplished. But that was a hard one, and they got us from right at the beginning.”× Arkansas head coach John Calipari looks on, Thursday, March 26, 2026, during the second half of the Razorbacks' 109-88 loss to the Arizona Wildcats in the NCAA Tournament Sweet 16 at SAP Center in San Jose, Calif. (Hank Layton/WholeHogSports) Arizona took a lead 18 seconds into the game and never trailed. After leading 54-43 at halftime, the Wildcats imposed their will in the second half and handed Arkansas what tied for the sixth-most lopsided loss in program history in an NCAA Tournament game.It was the most points scored against the Razorbacks in the postseason. Arkansas lost 108-77 to North Carolina in the second round in 2008.“I thought they came out and played with tremendous focus,” Arizona coach Tommy Lloyd said. “Locked in. Felt like long stretches of that game we couldn't get a stop. But it's one of those games where sometimes you've just got to keep scoring, keep putting the pressure on them, keep putting the pressure on them. I thought our guys did a good job of that.”The Wildcats had six players score at least 14 points and feasted in the paint, where they outscored the Razorbacks 60-50. Arizona averaged 42 paint points coming into the game, but went well above that mark with 15 layups and seven dunks.Koa Peat (21 points), Ivan Kharchenkov (15) and Tobe Awaka (14) had their way around the rim, where the Wildcats bullied the Razorbacks for much of the game.“A combination of physical play, along with size,” Calipari said. “Their duck-ins are more to move your men out of the way so they can shoot layups. And their bigs are big enough, if you don't do something, they can back you toward the basket and make shots.”× Arizona forward Koa Peat (10) makes a layup near teammate Motiejus Krivas (13) and Arkansas forward Trevon Brazile (7), Thursday, March 26, 2026, during the second half of the Razorbacks' 109-88 loss to the Wildcats in the NCAA Tournament Sweet 16 at SAP Center in San Jose, Calif. (Hank Layton/WholeHogSports) It was evident from the jump the Wildcats were going to get their way offensively, as they took a 26-15 lead by the second media timeout. They were shooting 77% from the field at that juncture, and the hot shooting never cooled much.Arizona was 37 for 58 (64%) from the field — the second-best field goal percentage in a Sweet 16 game since 2000.“They made a bunch of shots,” Calipari said. “That's the highest percentage that I can remember someone shooting. You have to admit, some of them bounced around and went in. You bang the 3 in the corner … we did everything right, bang, bang, boom, it went down. One of those kinds of days.”The early separation was maintained through the remainder of the first half, as Arizona built its lead to as much as 46-31 with 3:46 left in the half on a dunk by Awaka. The Razorbacks found some offensive flow over the half’s last few minutes but continued to struggle getting stops. The Wildcats didn’t let Arkansas go on any run greater than 4-0 in the first half.“Arizona was way better than us today,” Calipari said. “And I didn't think they'd be way better. I thought we could hang around. I knew it was a bad matchup because of their size. But they're good.”Arizona strengthened its grip on the lead early in the second half with a quick 11-4 run. It was capped by a Brayden Burries and-1 that was part of the guard’s team-best 23-point performance, and put the Wildcats ahead 65-47 with 17:17 to play.× Arkansas guard Darius Acuff (center) looks on near Arizona forward Dwayne Aristode (left), Arizona guard Brayden Burries (center, right) and Arkansas guard D.J. Wagner, Thursday, March 26, 2026, during the closing seconds of the Razorbacks' 109-88 loss to the Wildcats in the NCAA Tournament Sweet 16 at SAP Center in San Jose, Calif. (Hank Layton/WholeHogSports) “We started good in the second half, which was really important,” Lloyd said. “You don't get to push a button that says start good. The guys have to go out and do it. Sometimes they do, and sometimes you don't. Whichever way it happens, there's still a lot of game to be played.”After the Razorbacks fought to get within 14 points on free throws by Darius Acuff with 15:18 remaining, Arizona punched back with the game’s knockout run. A layup by Jaden Bradley and 3-pointer by Burries kickstarted a 9-2 run that put the Wildcats up 78-57 by the 13:19 mark. Arkansas never got closer than within 17 points the rest of the way.“Florida kind of did this same thing to us and for the same reason, because of their size,” Calipari said. “Of all the matchups that I didn't want to see, it was this one. I told my staff, ‘This is a bad matchup; let's figure out how we keep this thing in check. And then maybe if we're close, the pressure flips to them.’ We never made it where we could get it to [single digits] and flip the switch.”Frustration started to mount for the Razorbacks over the final stages of the second half while watching their season fade away. Fouls were a theme of the game, and Arizona had a 25-16 advantage in calls.Trevon Brazile picked up a Flagrant 1 foul going for an offensive rebound, Nick Pringle was assessed a technical for bouncing the ball high after a foul call, and Billy Richmond was ejected with a Flagrant 2 call on what appeared to be a flop by Kharchenkov.The final technical foul call of the game went to Calipari with 5:38 remaining for something said from the bench. For the remainder of the game, Calipari did not speak to the referees.“We knew the game had potential to get like that,” Lloyd said. “They had a game against Florida a few weeks back, there were a bunch of technical fouls swayed both ways. We've had a few instances this year where it's been a bit of a melee, and we've participated in it as well.“We want to play championship basketball. To play championship basketball, you've got to just stand up and walk away from the action. This isn't the playground. … You can't just throw down. That's not how you win basketball games.”× Arkansas head coach John Calipari reacts, Thursday, March 26, 2026, during the second half of the Razorbacks' 109-88 loss to the Arizona Wildcats in the NCAA Tournament Sweet 16 at SAP Center in San Jose, Calif. (Hank Layton/WholeHogSports) Arizona took a 25-point lead at 104-79 with 4:17 to play. Arkansas was led in scoring by Acuff (28 points), Meleek Thomas (17) and Richmond (13). Acuff, the SEC Player of the Year who is a projected lottery pick for the NBA Draft in June, likely played his final college game. “He was the ultimate competitor, had a will to win, would make baskets because he wasn't afraid to miss late in games,” Calipari said. “He and Meleek and the other guys, they set the stage for growth.”Box ScoreArizona 109, Arkansas 88.PDFHighlights
